div.head: 468. Memorandum of Conversation

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: Venezuelan President Herrera Campins and Secretary Haig Bilateral

list.label: Venezuela
list.item: Minister of the Presidency Garcia Bustillos

div.p: The following substantive issues were discussed during this meeting:

Herrera Campins said that at Cancun expectations had been created that the North/South global negotiations would go forward. It is important to consolidate what has been achieved by the setting and implementation of partial, concrete goals. One such place to begin would be assistance by the industrialized countries to the developing countries in food and agriculture, a theme that was flagged at Cancun. Another possibility would be the development of a special Inter-American Development Bank Trust fund which would help the private sector.
Since Cancun should be seen as a defeat for the Soviet Union, we must take advantage of the opportunity now before us. Secretary Haig responded that since Cancun President Reagan has begun steps to implement his commitment on agriculture. This involves consultations with other countries. Furthermore, Ambassador Kirkpatrick has been instructed to explore informally with all interested nations how we should go forward with the global negotiations. The experience at Cancun had a profound impact on President Reagan despite the difficulties. The US is optimistic that the spirit of Cancun will be an historic achievement. President Reagan is very much engaged and will welcome President Herrera’s observations.

Secretary Haig then moved to a discussion of the status of the CBI. A successful regional effort strengthens global negotiations. Not enough preparatory work had been done before the last ministerial meeting to give the CBI real shape. After January 1, President Reagan will announce important new efforts by the US in trade, investment and economic assistance. This should be kept confidential because the Congress and other interested groups have not yet been fully consulted. Our efforts reflect our concern about the Caribbean and Central America and we are convinced that the poor and hungry there need help in solving their problems, not just words. Unless we can relieve the social crisis, our security assistance will fail. If President Herrera can express concern about the economic crisis in the region while in the US, this could help convince the US Congress to provide the resources. Of course, it would also be useful for President Herrera to mention the security threat and aggression in the region. We hope that at a minimum President Herrera will not find it necessary to say anything which would hamper our efforts to get economic and security resources.

President Herrera noted that he believed time was on the side of democracy in El Salvador. He asked about some pessimistic statements attributed to the Secretary. The Secretary responded that we have a fine line to walk in painting a grave enough picture to get resources from the Congress while at the same time not making it seem so grave as to discourage our friends. The government
of El Salvador must understand that it has to go forward with elections. President Herrera commented that the military and right must receive no encouragement to interfere with free elections. His information was that even the hardest liners on the Salvadoran Right are beginning to accept this need. Secretary Haig reiterated our commitment to the election process. He added that it would be useful if the Venezuelan military could share the benefits of its anti-guerrilla experience in the 1960’s with the Salvadorans. We are worried because the Salvadoran military only reacts now and they should be taking initiatives as Venezuela did.

Secretary Haig said that we have become increasingly concerned in recent weeks about Nicaragua. The Nicaraguan Government is systematically eliminating its opposition. It is important that the other nations of the region appear as concerned about this as we are. We appreciate the Venezuelan reaction of diplomatic disapproval toward the Sandinistas and welcome Venezuelan ideas on how to deal with the problem. President Herrera said he was also concerned about Nicaragua and had made a declaration on the subject, as had Acting President Montes de Oca. While there is severe pressure on the democratic forces, information indicates that the time may be approaching when the democratic countries of the hemisphere can undertake a political step to reverse the trend there. The GRN is susceptible to international pressure. Nicaragua is not lost; the door must be kept open for those Nicaraguan forces which are fighting for pluralism. We should not leave them alone. For example, help must be given to the press which is being strangled economically and to free radio stations to keep them operating. Venezuela realizes that what happens in Nicaragua and elsewhere will have its effect throughout the continent.

The Secretary said that we had gone ahead with the notification to Congress of the F–16 sale to Venezuela on Thursday, November 12, and that we expect approval of this without major difficulties because Venezuela is such a highly regarded democracy. We are also committed to try to deliver the first aircraft before President Herrera leaves office.
This issue, Secretary Haig noted, is one of the few bilateral problems between us. It would be useful if President Herrera could help find some solution.

It was mentioned by Secretary Haig that sometimes friends dwell too much on their areas of difference and too little on their many areas of agreement. We deeply value our friendship with Venezuela. Because of Venezuela’s democratic history and its influence in the region, it can do much that we cannot. We don’t want to burden Venezuela with a requirement of endorsement of our policy. It is more important that our values converge. We sincerely welcome advice and criticism from Venezuela and President Reagan is looking forward to fuller exploration of several of the subjects discussed above in his talks with President Herrera. President Herrera said that one of the attributes of friendship is that one can talk about everything frankly.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, Roger W. Fontaine Files, Subject File, Venezuela [October 1981–November 1981]. Confidential. Drafted on November 17 by Hart; cleared by Haig, Luers, and in S/S. Goldberg signed for Haig. The meeting took place at Blair House. In telegram 10292 from Caracas, October 30, the Embassy sent briefing information for Herrera’s visit. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810514–0990) Herrera made a State visit to Washington, November 16–19.

According to the President’s Daily Diary, Reagan met with Herrera October 21 at the Cancun Summit conference on North-South issues. (Reagan Library, President’s Daily Diary) No memorandum of conversation has been found.

See Document 466. In a November 6 action memorandum from Enders, Fairbanks, and Burt, Buckley approved their recommendation that Congress be informally notified on November 12 of the F–16 sale to Venezuela. (Reagan Library, Jacqueline Tillman Files, Subject File, Venezuela 11/07/1981)
